utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have just received a translation for D432 that was MFI'd, and therefore I would seek to tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- document that will become Exhibit 432, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, just a slight digression. After the signing of the agreement with Mr. Byrnes in October 1998, have you ever met him after that date?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have Exhibit P703.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness's both mikes be switched on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, this is 113 in your binder. This is a dispatch of the 31st of December, 1998, or rather, a letter signed in your name. Can you tell us briefly what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are some clarifications that were distributed to all the secretariats, and they relate to the procedure of the employment procedure for the employees of the MUP. The main message in this letter was that the vetting procedures that had been in place before from henceforth would be done by the Secretariat of the Interior, whereas some other vetting that were on the archive of the State Security Service would be used in individual cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now have document P1205. It's dated the 15th of January, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It's your tab 114. Can you tell us the content of this dispatch, please.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This dispatch as well as some previous ones referred to in this dispatch relate to primarily the transportation of foodstuffs, medicines, oil derivatives, et cetera, in the area of both Serbia and into Kosovo and Metohija. There's also information contained therein that the Government of Serbia had adopted certain decisions in order to improve the supply of these staple necessities in Kosovo and Metohija. This implies the information -- the obligation that have to be undertaken by the secretariats and the public security units in order to effect the control of these goods delivered to Kosovo in order to prevent any kind of abuse, that is to say that it's been delivered to its true recipient. This is the dispatch sent to all the secretariats and all to the public security units.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain in more detail the penultimate paragraph on page 2 which reads that it is necessary that the regional secretariats covering the roads and the check-points towards the AP KiM and Montenegro should step-up control of passengers, luggage, and vehicles. Which particular secretariat does this refer to?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We spoke about this earlier. In the past, there was an order issued to the secretariat that are close to Kosovo, especially the Pec secretariat which is on the border with Montenegro, to establish check-points in order to control passengers, luggage, and probably stop any smuggle of deficiency goods such as weapons and ammunition. These check-points had been set up previously, and, in this letter, it is said that a better control should be in place in order to prevent smuggling and possible abuse of import of this stuffs that were in shortage.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us which particular secretariat this referred to.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were Novi Pazar, Leskovac, Vranje, that is to say, the secretariats. I -- also Prokuplje was included there as well, but only five or six of them that were close to the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now look document D001-2910, that's 1205 according to 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And in your binder it's 115. Mr. Djordjevic, what were you doing on the 15th of January, 1999, can you recall?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 15th of January, 1999, I came to work as usual and I sent this dispatch that we have just discussed. After that, according to previous tasks received from the minister, together with him and other members of the government I went to Kosovo because the Government of the Republic of Serbia had decided that on that day they were going to hold their meeting in Pristina. So pursuant to the minister's order, I was part of that delegation. And sometime during the morning we set off. Some members of the government flew, some road in a car. Anyway, the meeting was convened for 1200 hours in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: How did you travel to Pristina?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I flew together with the minister. And at the Pristina airport we were met by the head of the MUP staff, General Sreten Lukic; and after that, we went to the meeting of the government. I attended this meeting. It had its agenda, and there was certain topics discussed there. After the government which didn't last -- after the meeting, which didn't last long, we went to the premises where the MUP staff was housed, and with top officials of the secretariat and the staff from Kosovo and Metohija, we had a meeting attended by the prime minister and the vice prime ministers who were on the delegation of the government as well as some politicians from Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember what was discussed at this particular meeting?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, basically this was a meeting that the Government of Serbia used practically to render its support to the police forces that were carrying out very responsible tasks down there. That was a standard meeting dedicated to this topic, short information or report was given on the security situation; and after that the prime minister addressed the meeting by giving his support. That was the topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, do you remember who submitted the support on the -- the report on the security situation on -- in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This short outline of the security situation was submitted by the head of the staff, which was the usual practice whenever other officials attended such kind of meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What did you do next on the 15th of January?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After this meeting held at the MUP staff premises, the delegation went for lunch; I was there as well. After the lunch, the prime minister and the minister of the interior went back to Belgrade, whereas the other members of delegation continued their work according to the preset schedule. What was important at that point was, when I came to the room where we were supposed to have lunch, Goran Radosavljevic, member of the staff, informed me in passing that there had been an action carried out in order to arrest terrorists in the village of Racak, and that in that action there were terrorists killed. I received this piece of information as something utterly unofficial that he imparted on me, but given that the minister and other members were already at lunch, I informed them about this incident that Goran Radosavljevic told me about without giving any numbers or going into any details. I just conveyed what he told me in passing. After the lunch, as I said, the prime minister and the minister left for Belgrade, and all the rest of us remained there in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that a terrorist action was to be carried out before Mr. Radosavljevic told you about it?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not a terrorist action, that was an anti-terrorist action. Of course I didn't know about it, because I had just arrived from Belgrade on that morning. That was an action of a completely local character and, as he put it at the time, this was only about arresting terrorists that had inflicted considerable losses in the previous day on the police force, and their activities resulted in the blockade of main roads. Therefore, I had heard nothing about any plan for such an action, but after the minister and other delegation members had left on the premises of the staff, because I didn't receive any further information, I wanted to know what the situation was and what actually had happened in Racak. The people and the staff told me these few things, that this was an action of such a nature and its objective was to apprehend the terrorists for whom there was intelligence that they were in a specific house in Racak. The entire action was designed by the Secretariat of the Interior in Urosevac with the participation of the staff, and, according to some previous obligations that were laid down, the plan was made by the secretariat in Urosevac. It was verified by the staff, and the staff itself in accordance with its obligations towards the verification mission was duty-bound to notify the verification mission that such an action with a view to apprehending a group of terrorists in a village was to be carried out. That is when they told me that they had notified the verification mission about the impending action. Actually, they did it on the day before, and they said that the action was to take place on the 15th. What they also told me was that towards the end of this action and the settling of accounts with these terrorists, a fierce counter-attack was launched by the terrorist forces which had regrouped in the neighbouring villages. And they managed to push back the police, and practically the police had to leave the area and the area remained under the control of terrorist forces. Therefore, the staff didn't have any further information either about the consequences of this anti-terrorist action or, let's say, the action to arrest the terrorist group that was in the village. That's what they told me on that evening. This is all I know about the action of the 15th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: On the 15th of January, 1999, did you go to Stimlje?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I already described what I did on that day, and I didn't go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: On the 15th of January, did anyone mention to you any civilian casualties resulting from the Racak action?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody at the staff at that time knew anything about the number of casualties and who they were, what gender they were of. So, in other words, the staff had no detailed information. All they knew that there were casualties. On the 15th, they didn't have this information available. After the action or towards its action, they told me that they had attempted to carry out an on-site investigation in the village but that was impossible because the police forces had practically left the area under the pressure of the terrorists. Therefore, no investigation could have done on that day. What the staff knew was just general information, but they had no specifics.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you did on the 16th of January, 1999?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to plan, along with the government delegation consisting of, among others, vice prime ministers, I went to Prizren. This delegation had some political meetings, as planned before, and the next meeting was in Pec attended by the local politicians as well. We flew in a helicopter to Prizren, and after that I returned to Pristina. And with Ratko Markovic, the vice prime minister, I went to Pec where I attended these political talks and meetings that the government delegation had in the area. In the early evening or late afternoon after the talks had finished, I went back to Pristina. I had some previous arrangements, and I also agreed that, with the minister, to go to Mount Kapaonik where I also had a meeting, and I wanted to take advantage of the forthcoming weekend to spend some time skiing. On the 16th, after I had finished all the business that I had with the government, I asked Savo Stalevic, who was the commander of the Pristina special unit, and since I had come by airplane and I didn't have a car to take me to Mount Kapaonik, to drive me there because this is not far from Pristina. We had this meeting there, which he attended as well, and on the morning of the next day, we spent time skiing with them at Mount Kapaonik. So that was on the 16th and, let's say, by midday on the 17th is how I spent my time in Kosovo and how I went to Kapaonik after Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any information on the 16th about the Racak incident?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had to leave immediately after the meeting in Pec for Kapaonik, so practically on that day I didn't receive any information about what had happened in Racak or about the situation in Kosovo in general as well as in Serbia with relation to the Racak action.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that the KVM head, Mr. Walker, held a press conference; and if you did know, where were you when you learned of that?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned that when I watched TV on Kapaonik later on in the evening, on the news. I simply acknowledged that information without any particular measures on my part or any particular interest concerning that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What did you learn next about the Racak events, and what did you do about it?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around noon or 1.00 p.m., I received a phone call from the minister. He called me on my mobile and ordered me to go to Pristina because the situation grew more complex and that I should assist if needed in order to clear up the situation concerning Racak. Following that phone call and his order, I also received a phone call from Sreten Lukic who told me that he would be sending a helicopter to pick me up. An hour or two later, the helicopter indeed arrived; and sometime in the afternoon, on the minister's orders, I returned to the staff. It was there that I was informed in detail about everything that was at the disposal of the staff by that point in time. I was told that there had been an operation and everything else that I shared with you that was told to me on the 15th. I was also told that they attempted to carry out an on-site investigation, both on the 16th and the 17th, but that the team was unable to conduct it due to terrorist attacks. I was also told that on the 17th of January the police station was attacked as well as some other facilities nearby. The head of the staff advised me that on the minister's orders a plan was drafted to go back to the area of the village of Racak in order to ascertain what the situation is, what had taken place indeed, and whether there were any killed, and also to secure the location for the on-site investigation team to do their work. I was told that the plan was drawn up and that according to the plan the next morning, in the morning, they should go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. While you were in Pristina and the staff concerning Mr. Walker's press conference, did you receive any information about the targets of those activities and who the victims were?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was informed in detail about what Mr. Walker said at the press conference. He called it a civilian massacre and I was also given all the other information. The head of the staff also told me that the minister was greatly concerned as well as many other senior officials in Serbia in relation to the event and that everyone is interested in learning what the situation was and to see whether what Mr. Walker said at the press conference is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What information did the staff have concerning the victims of this anti-terrorist operation?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to that time, that is to say, on the 17th in the late afternoon, the staff did not have any information about the casualties in detail because the territory was still practically under KLA control. The only information we had was the information that came from Mr. Walker.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That was Mr. Walker's information. What information did the staff have about the activities undertaken and about what took place in Racak?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not understand the question. The staff knew what the activities undertaken were. And I told you already, there was an anti-terrorist operation according to a pre-set plan and the obligations we had towards the verification mission. I was trying to tell you that at that point in time the staff was not aware of the consequences. They didn't know what the casualties were, what kind of persons they were, because we had no control over the territory, the police that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During the rest of your stay in Pristina, what followed?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning, on the 18th of January, when the operation of returning to Racak village began, I went to the Stimlje police station since I wanted to see for myself what the situation was and to see what the effects of the entering of the police force to Racak were. I came upon the chief of the SUP as well as his assistant there. I came across an on-site investigation team headed by an investigative judge and an autopsy expert, Dr. Dobricanin, as well as deputy county prosecutor from Urosevac. In the police station, a scene-of-crime team was put together that was to accompany the other staff to the location. I also noticed the damage on the police station building sustained during the attack on the previous day, that is to say, the 17th. Before noon or around noon, the police entered Racak village. In the mosque they found lined up bodies. Information about that was sent to the chief of the SUP, and I was on the premises as well. The entire territory was under police control by that time and the chief advised the investigating judge of that who was there as well, whereupon the judge set out with the entire team of judiciary officials as well as police to carry out an on-site investigation. Since the police had access to the territory, it was possible to ascertain what had taken place and who the casualties were. I went to the staff, after which I returned to Belgrade. Concerning the information the chief of the secretariat received about the situation in the village and the bodies found, he sent that information on to the MUP staff because they were very interested in receiving any new piece of information. According to my knowledge, the investigating judge, while I was still in Pristina, issued an order for the bodies to be sent to the forensic department in Pristina. I also know that the paraffin glove prints were taken and the rest of the procedure was under the control of the investigative and judicial authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you inform the minister upon your return to Belgrade about what you have learned while in Pristina, or did you do that while you were still in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke with him on the phone from Pristina, but the head of the staff advised him before I did based on the information he had received from the SUP chief. I also told him of what I saw down there, and I suggested that I go back to Belgrade. He accepted that, as there were no further reasons for my stay. There is one thing I would like to point out that has to do with my stay in the Stimlje Police Station. In the overall activities which were there to enable an on-site investigation and in order to put the territory under police control, the terrorists killed the assistant station commander in Urosevac, Mr. Mekic. While I was there, his brother-in-law --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Father-in-law.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- came in. He was very bitter at having learned of his son-in-law's death. It was a very grave situation that I was witness to. After that, I returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Based on all the investigating procedures and information you had, what were you basically told about what had happened in Racak?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the initial and subsequent detailed analyses that were carried out as well after the autopsies that were undertaken by the judiciary, it was ascertained that the wounds sustained by the victims did not indicate that a crime had been committed or that they were liquidated or shot point-blank. It was ascertained, rather, that those were gun-shot wounds characteristic of combat and combat activities in general. In other words, these would be usual injuries that people sustained in conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could D001-2910 be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you please go to tab 119 next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The document will be received, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D437.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Next, I would kindly ask for P139.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Which is tab 119 in your binder. Mr. Djordjevic, this is a dispatch of the 16th of February, 1999. It contains your first and last name, but someone signed for you. Can you tell us what the dispatch is about, briefly.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This dispatch was sent on the 16th of February to certain SUPs as well as detachment commanders and the staff in Pristina and the joint affairs administration in the ministry. This is a standard type of dispatch which follows a minister decision on the engagement of certain units in order to send new units to the field or to replace the units which are already in the field. The secretariats are requested to provide for additional units to be engaged. This is a standard type dispatch without which the units could not be sent in the field. It contains all the details we have already discussed. These are, so to say, technical obligations that have to be undertaken by the secretariats and the joint affairs administration in the ministry, so as to enable those units to depart ready to conduct their special tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we next go to P85.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Tab 120.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 17th of February, the minister, together with the most senior officials of both the state and public security services, visited the MUP staff in Pristina. He held a meeting with all members of the ministry engaged in the staff. General Sreten Lukic briefed them on the security situation, and other participants in the meeting reported on their respective areas of responsibility, which was followed in turn by a longer address of the minister. He first addressed certain political aspects and the news among the politicians as well as issued detailed orders on the conduct of the Ministry of the Interior as well as the staff and its organisational units in the area of Kosovo and Metohija. These were detailed orders that were later on followed by the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Djordjevic, on the first page in both versions, we see the words of General Lukic, and then in the seventh line from the bottom in the Serbian version it says: "A plan of the RJB has been worked out to prevent and hinder the entry of NATO troops into our territory. The staff planned when this is ordered to carry out three mopping-up operations in the areas of Podujevo, Dragobilje, and Drenica areas." Can you tell us what this is about? What is it that General Lukic speaks about here?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the earlier dispatch that I sent on the 7th of October, when there was a threat of bombing looming over us, we saw that there was an order to bring up-to-date all defence plans. And here, again, when it was completely obvious that a NATO offensive was about to occur with a great likelihood of them coming in with land forces into our territory, the duty of the RJB was vis-à-vis the plans on activities aimed at hindering the entry of NATO forces to work on those plans. All of those plans were to be brought up-to-date, and they also had to ensure personnel, especially those from reserve forces, so as to be ready for the entry of enemy land forces. And then in later documents we saw that, for the other parts of Serbia, similar orders were being issued as well as orders on linking up with the army in order to respond properly to this offensive. There was some indications that NATO forces would enter from other areas, not just from the territory of Albania or Macedonia. So that is what this plan was about, and what he spoke of here could only pertain to that particular situation. Other than that, that's what it was. The RJB had a plan dealing with this situation. This was a general plan as developed by the Ministry of the Interior on how to proceed in that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But it says here that the staff planned to do this once it was ordered. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, as to what the staff planned, that wasn't something that the staff could have received from the RJB. I know that the staff could only act based on the plans developed at that point in time by the army. I'm not aware of any particular planning activities of the staff, and I don't know who this order was supposed to come from. So it is not clear to me what the head of the staff meant when he reported on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now at which point in time did the head of the staff say - and also in relation to which situation did he say - that this would happen?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basic approach here is that should there be an attack by terrorists launched in Podujevo, Dragobilje, and Drenica areas, and there was also this looming attack of NATO forces, that at that point in time they were to be engaged in mopping-up or sweeping activities in order to get rid of terrorists in that area. This was done because there was a lot of terrorists in that area and also in order to do a quality work on defence preparations. First they had to neutralise the terrorists in that area so as to prevent them from potentially assisting the enemy forces once they entered into the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was that plan to be applied if NATO forces did not enter our territory?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that an operation of such a large volume and with so many participants would not be conducted had there not been this expectation that NATO forces would enter the territory and that there would be a bombing campaign.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now could we see the last page of the B/C/S version of the document and in the English version as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The third bullet point from the bottom, we see that in his address the minister stated that SAJ should be included more effectively and engaged.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see that at that point in time he issued a lot of detailed orders, and, in this particular situation, he had information that the SAJ was not included in the most efficient manner in the preparations and in the activities. And in that context, he says that there should be more effective inclusion and engagement of the SAJ in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have P5356.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Which is tab 121 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a dispatch --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. This is Exhibit P356, and this is a dispatch of the 18th of February, 1999, dispatch number 312. On the last page we can see that you signed it. Can you briefly explain the content and significance of this dispatch.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is dated 18th of February, 1999. It was evident at that point in time that there would be a military aggression carried out against FRY by NATO alliance, and based on that assessment, as well as orders that the minister gave on the previous day to everybody who were at the staff in Kosovo, I sent this dispatch to all organisational units first of all within the seat of the ministry and then to all chiefs of SUPs, to the staff in Pristina, to the border crossing police stations where it says 1-35, to the commander, and also to the state security department for them to be informed of this. So here you see detailed instructions concerning preparations for defence against the potential aggression, as well as in case that terrorist activities from Kosovo spread out into the rest of the territory of Serbia. And further on it says that the defence plans should be brought up-to-date with a focus on preparations for being on alert, preparations for mobilisations, and defence preparations. Further on, they -- this document speaks of various duties in all fields of work of the ministry in order to tell them how to conduct preparations for the upcoming attack. What you can also see here is an order that all secretariats need to plan relocation from their regular premises, and there's a number of other tasks within all lines of work of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see page 2 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And as for you, Mr. Djordjevic, you can look at item 7. I think it's page 2 for you as well. Could you comment on item 7, please.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This item specifies that there should be a stepped-up control or intensified control over existing paramilitary and other formations who had participated in various conflicts in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. So what this item speaks of is that through intensified intelligence and other measures and actions, they should prevent the departure or stay of such units in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see D004-1675.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, we will see a dispatch dated the 2nd of March, 1999. So can you just briefly tell us what the purpose of this dispatch was.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the previous dispatch, we saw that it was ordered that there should be constant duty services established in all municipal units, in all regional secretariats, and so on; and then it was decided that it was too much of a burden for the senior personnel, following which it was ordered that they should be on passive duty shifts and that all other measures remained as earlier so that, in a way, their task became lighter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did we say to whom this dispatch was sent?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just like previous dispatch, 312, it was sent to all organisational units. So it followed the basic dispatch. So all of those entities that received the previous dispatch also received this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see D010 -- I apologise. Could the previous document please be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D438.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now see D010-0317. It's 1203 under Rule 65 ter motion of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It's tab 123 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a letter --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: No, no, I apologise. We have a wrong document. So 00128 -- 0022879. It's 1203 on the 65 ter list, D001-2879. That's the one.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a letter sent by the minister to the Deputy Prime Minister, Nikola Sainovic, who was the chairman of the commission on co-operation with the OSCE, the one that we mentioned earlier. So Knut Vollebaek sent some complaints to Zivadin Jovanovic, minister of foreign affairs, complaints on a lack of -- on the fact that the Ministry of Foreign Affairs did not abide by certain previously agreed provisions, and then the minister wrote a letter to him individually addressing each of these complaints. The staff verified the complaints from that information and then sent, in turn, the information to the minister, explaining in detail each particular instance. The office of the minister received this information from this staff, and here the minister forwarded it to the chairman of the state commission for co-operation with the OSCE, who -- which was Nikola Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have this admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D439.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have P716.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Which is tab 124 in your binder. Mr. Djordjevic, this is a dispatch dated 16th of March, 1999, where you are listed as the sender. Could you just briefly tell us -- just a minute so that we have the English version on the screen. It's all right now.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a dispatch that was sent to all SUPs, to the staff in Pristina, and to all chiefs within the specialty lines of work, within the seat of the RJB at the ministry. And it deals with the residence and domicile of the citizens, all citizens, because at that point in time in Serbia there were a lot of refugees and internally displaced persons living there who had not completely regulated their status, as a result of which this dispatch was sent with instructions on what to do in such situations. So this is a dispatch dealing with routine tasks concerning registering citizens, drawing up appropriate lists, identification papers of citizens, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, we have a dispatch here of the 18th of March. Can we please look the exhibit. Yes, we have it. Mr. Djordjevic, with regard to this dispatch of the 18th of March, 1999, could you please comment on it and tell us what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a usual dispatch relating to the sending or rotation of members --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What's the exhibit number, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's P137. So it's dated the 18th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one of the many that had been sent before or after. It relates to the obligations of secretariats, that elements of their units should be dispatched. And they are informing the MUP staff as well, the secondary school in Sremska Kamenica as well - because they had buses at their disposals which were, at the time, used, quite frequently, to take members to Kosovo. So this is a standard dispatch that, as I said, had been sent many times before and later to the competent secretariats in order to act accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now look at P138.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, we see the same date, only the reference number is different. Can you tell us in the briefest possible terms what this dispatch is about.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This dispatch was sent to other secretariats compared to the previous ones. Everything else is the same. It is only sent to the secretariats that have to act accordingly, that is to say, Kragujevac, Zajecar, and Pristina secretariats, and the command of the detachment in Kragujevac, as well as the staff in Pristina. As for the rest, it's identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now look at Exhibit P1206.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, this is a dispatch of the 22nd of March, 1999, that you signed personally. Let us just wait for a second before it appears. And it's your tab 127. Can you tell us, briefly.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a dispatch sent on the 22nd of March, which is immediately before the commencement of the bombing, in which all the SUPs and border police stations as well as organisational units within the ministry head office are instructed, in compliance with a general dispatch 312 of the 18th of February, to act in accordance and to activate all the measures because the attack on Yugoslavia was about to take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now look at Exhibit D258.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It's your tab 128. Mr. Djordjevic, let us just be patient until it appears on our screens. Mr. Djordjevic, what we see here is a dispatch dated the 22nd March, 1999, signed by the head of the administration, Major-General Slobodan Spasic. Can you tell us who this person is, and what's the essence of this dispatch?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This dispatch was also sent on the eve of the war itself by the head of the administration of fire-fighting police, who, in compliance with his duties and responsibilities, instructed all the SUPs to intensify their work in order to engage members of the territorial fire-fighting units. These territorial fire-fighting units were under the professional leadership of this particular chief or this administration. Now, in view of the fact that an attack was imminent in which the territorial fire-fighting units would have a special role, the head of this administration wanted them to be fully prepared to carry out their fire-fighting work properly. And he also instructed other measures to be undertaken with regard to providing supplies to the civilians with water and other needs that this particular service can provide.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we now have a new binder given to the accused containing various copies of documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, our last evidence was a telegram of the 22nd of March, 1999. What I'd like to know is, immediately before the war began and when the state of an imminent threat of war was conveyed, were any meetings held at the ministry; and if yes, what kind of meetings?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course that meeting was held there. The minister and his assistants in charge of various lines of work met, and there was general discussion about the obligations imposed by the previous dispatch number 312. On the 24th, the minister, in view of the fact that the state of war had already been declared, this dispatch described the danger of Yugoslavia coming under attack; however, the situation was different now, and the federal government had proclaimed a state of war. Consequently, the minister, in his dispatch dated the 24th, ordered additional measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We haven't come to that yet. Can you please wait a second. Can you tell us at that meeting what kind of discussion was held, and were any specific tasks issued with regard to the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A discussion was held about the obligations of all organisational units concerning the impending war. And after the meeting, the minister invited to his office Mr. Obrad Stevanovic -- General Stevanovic, and myself, where he gave us specific tasks and assignments for the forthcoming period. That is when he told General Obrad, who had been told at the previous meeting where the NATO forces would be concentrated, he said to General Obrad Stevanovic at this meeting that the most serious activity would be taking place in the area of Kosovo and Metohija; that the staff that had already been set up by the minister should continue its activities as before, but that in view of a large number of manpower engaged down there and the very complex situation that was anticipated, he instructed Obrad to go to Kosovo and help them there and convey the minister's order in order to be able for us to respond to this highly complex security situation. This is also when he told Obrad that, in accordance with his responsibilities, he would be answerable to him for the uniformed forces, and the majority of these forces through special units were already engaged down there. And he told Obrad that since he was very well familiar with the situation down there, it was necessary for him to stay in Kosovo and Metohija for the ministry and to operate successfully and for the task to be completed. At that -- on that occasion, he told me that my duty was to be in charge of regular public security work, but he gave me a particular assignment of maintaining a 24-hour contact with all heads of the SUPs and that their responsibilities that stemmed from the previous dispatches should be monitored by me as well as the activities that they -- that the NATO pact was carrying out in their respective areas. So my particular responsibility related only to the SUPs within [as interpreted] Kosovo and Metohija when it comes to NATO attacks. In other words, everything else that concerned the territory outside of Kosovo and Metohija became my responsibility. And in that respect, the heads of the SUPs briefed me about all the problems that they were facing in their respective areas about each air-strike and about any action that had to be taken in every specific situation. So from that moment on until the end of the war, I was constantly in communication with all these heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just for the record, Mr. Djordjevic, can you tell me which particular SUPs according to minister's orders were you responsible for?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was responsible for, according to minister's orders, to the SUPs outside of the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The record shows that the minister assigned you the duty of being responsible for the secretariats inside the Kosovo and Metohija. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Djordjevic, from the 24th of March, 1999, onwards - that is to say until the withdrawal from the Kosovo and Metohija territory by the SUP and police forces - were you in contact with the heads of the SUPs in Kosovo and Metohija except when you were there on the ground?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The NATO air-strikes were carried out on a daily basis against the whole territory of Serbia, and they were particularly frequent on the areas of secretariats outside of Kosovo. I was in contact with them on a daily basis. As for the heads of the secretariats in Kosovo and Metohija, I never spoke to them during the NATO air campaign, that is to say, they had their own communications channels for sending information. And all other heads of secretariats were obliged to keep in touch with me. And I used to call them a few times a day, depending on the problems that they faced in their respective areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we, please, now see Exhibit P702.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, we see the minister's dispatch of the 23rd of March, 1999, or we shall see it shortly. That one --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the number of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Tell us briefly about this dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's Exhibit P702.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we see it on the screen. On the 23rd of March, 1999, is sending this dispatch to heads of the lines in the ministry head office in all secretariats and all commanders of border patrol units and the SUP headquarters. In it he informs them that the federal government on the 23rd of March had declared a state of war or an imminent threat of war, and practically he is ordering them to act in accordance with the previous orders -- order contained in dispatch 312 sent on the 18th. Basically, he reminded them of their general obligations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have Exhibit D237, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, we have another dispatch dated the 24th of March, 1999. Can you please tell us, very briefly, what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a dispatch sent just before the bombing. The bombing started that same evening. It was sent to both the state and public security services, to all chiefs of SUPs, the staff in Pristina, and all the border patrol stations. This contains a decision relating to special measures that the Government of Serbia had adopted with relation to the proclamation of a state of war. And it contains the obligations of all organs and organisations of the Government of Serbia, including some of the obligations of the Ministry of the Interior. In that respect, the minister had ordered the services in -- within the ministry to act in accordance with the Government of Serbia's decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we next have D238, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, it is tab 131 in your binder. It's a dispatch of the 25th of March, 1999, by Minister Vlajko Stojiljkovic. Could you tell us briefly what it's about.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the first day of bombardment, the next day he sent this dispatch specifying measures in order to step up operational work as well as the mobilisation of the reserve forces and to engage fire-fighting police units as well as fire-fighting crews in general. He proposed specific measures to all Public Security Service departments after day one of the bombing campaign.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have D255 next.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, it is tab 132 in your binder. A dispatch of the 26th of March, 1999, signed by Major-General Dragan Ilic, head of administration. Can you tell us who he is and what was the purpose of the dispatch as well as who it was sent to.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was sent by the crime police administration head, Major-General Ilic, on the 26th of March to all the SUPs in Serbia as well as the MUP staff in Pristina. In the dispatch, he warns of possible speculations and illegal trading with certain types of food that was -- that they were short of, as well as the manipulation with prices. It was his role to follow such issues, and he proposed measures to be taken if such black-market measures are detected. This is more or less part of his regular duties as the head of the crime police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's look at paragraph 2 of the dispatch. Could you please read that and comment.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we have already dealt with this dispatch. It seems that it was basically the minister who had issued an order by a previous dispatch, and Mr. Ilic is now forwarding that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next could we please have 65 ter document 4063.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This dispatch --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Djordjevic. This is a dispatch of the 27th of March, 1999, signed by Major-General Stojan Misic. What was his job at the time, and what's the gist of this dispatch?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The dispatch was sent by Major-General Stojan Misic, assistant minister to the federal interior ministry, and all the SUPs as well as the Pristina staff and border police stations and to the organisational units in the seat of the ministry. The dispatch deals with the issue of bringing up-to-date of all lists of foreigners with a permanent residence as well as issuing travel documents to military conscripts. It also regulates certain status matters. The assistant minister was answerable to the minister for his part of work. It has to do with personal documentation as well as the issue of status of certain citizens as well as foreign nationals in Serbia. On this occasion, he instructed the SUPs, given that the federal government decision on the proclamation of a state of war had taken place, he proposes measures to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe it is time for a break, but before that I would seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D440.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will break now and resume at 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would kindly ask for D253.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In your binder it is tab 134, Mr. Djordjevic. Let us wait a second until it appears on the screen. This is a dispatch of the 27th of March, 1999. Tell us briefly who it was sent to and what its purpose was.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The dispatch was sent on the 27th of March by the Assistant Minister Stojan Misic to all organisational units of the public security sector as well as the MUP staff. It deals with the issue of the role of locators in the bombing of ground targets. In order to have precise strikes, NATO air force made use of locators placed in the vicinity of facilities to be bombed. Stojan Misic sent this dispatch, advising the organisational units of that and instructing them how to behave should they come across locators and how to disable them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us go back to page 1, please. Mr. Djordjevic, something is illegible here or at least I don't see who drafted this. We see "assistant minister" but not what follows. However, on this cover page it says that this was a dispatch from the chief of the public security department or service.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the dispatch itself, one cannot see the signature, but -- well, I don't exclude the possibility that I sent it. In any case, I am fully familiar with the situation and with our instructions to the secretariats concerning locators.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Djordjevic, can you tell us what were the operational capacities of the Special Anti-Terrorist Unit at the beginning of the war in 1999?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards the end of the previous year, that is to say, 1998, the minister of the interior disbanded a part of the SAJ. There were some issues remaining from their previous engagements, therefore the operational capability of the SAJ under such circumstances was significantly reduced as pointed out by the minister himself during the meeting at which the unit commander was present, when he stated that their activities up to that point were insufficient and that they should step-up their activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We see in the decision on the formation of the SAJ that there had been three units at the beginning of the war or in the previous period, rather. At the beginning of the war, how many SAJ units were there?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war, what was left were two anti-terrorist units: the one in Belgrade and the one in Pristina, as well as the commanding staff headed by Mr. Trajkovic. Those were the forces of the Special Anti-Terrorist Unit of the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the SAJ have its own reserve force?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SAJ did not have its reserve force because the type of tasks of the specific tasks that they were supposed to be used for was such that the most trained and best members of the professional force are needed. All those tasks, even under regular circumstances, could have been undertaken by the professional members of the SAJ. However, when this unit is engaged in wartime conditions, the problem is, as we have said, that a part of the unit had been disbanded as well as that some of its members could not -- could no longer be used in combat at the time due to injuries. The second problem was that it did not have its own reserve force to man the unit to its full capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who was responsible for the situation in the unit?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person responsible for the situation in any unit, including an SAJ unit, is the commander. He needs to be aware of the tasks that are before his unit and needs to undertake all measures necessary to have the unit ready in terms of personnel and equipment in order to fulfil the tasks expected of them. At the meeting, the minister warned that the unit should be used more efficiently. After that, the commander of that unit, relying on his obligations received from the minister, wanted to make the unit better prepared in order to carry out tasks in wartime conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said "at that meeting," which meeting did you have in mind and when did it take place? You said at that meeting the minister warned of something.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The meeting took place on the 17th of February, 1999, in the MUP staff facilities in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about other units which fell within the public security sector, did they have their reserve forces and how did it function, how did those units -- reserve units function?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area of regional and municipal secretariats, there were so-called wartime units of those secretariats and municipal departments as well as separate units in the areas of those secretariats. All those war units and separate units had their reserve force, which, within the framework of general preparations of all the units, when trained for wartime circumstances, had been designated. Any police unit which had its reserve force had people appointed to it, and those people underwent certain training. Therefore, one could say that according to the plan, all units were manned by both professional personnel and reserve personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This was on a tangent because we were discussing the topic of commanders being responsible for the units. What about Mr. Trajkovic, the SAJ commander, did he have any contact with you, and did he undertake any measures in order to secure sufficient staffing of the SAJ?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After the meeting that we have just discussed or a few days later, he came to see me. He acquainted me with the situation and the issues in the unit concerning the total number of men he could raise for the forthcoming activities. On that occasion, he said that he needed first and foremost to have people not in order to carry out combat activities since the professional part of the SAJ was tasked with that; rather, he wanted to have men to secure the territory that had been taken by the professional force. They were also needed to secure accommodation for the entire unit so that the professional staff could have more rest time for any ensuing combat activities. He pointed out that particular problem. He said that with the number of men he had at his disposal, he wouldn't be able to meet the expectations and orders of the minister. He suggested that the unit be reinforced with certain reserve forces, the task of which would be as I have just stipulated. We were both aware that, within the overall structure, he had no ability to engage any reserve forces on his own. I agreed with his proposal that he try to come up with a number of men who could be engaged and that we were to discuss their ways and means of engagement later on. In that regard, he did undertake certain steps, and later he came to see me again. He said that he had some men, some of whom he had known since his engagement in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Sirmium, as the territory was used. He said they had experience, and they could be used for the tasks which he considered them to do. He suggested that they should be used to compensate for the shortage of staff in the SAJ. The only possibility was to have them brought into the MUP reserve force and later on seconded to the SAJ. As far as the information went, he had about a hundred men he could use. And I used that information to acquaint the minister with the situation in the SAJ and to propose to him what the commander had suggested on how to resolve the shortage of staff. The minister decided that those men be engaged as a MUP reserve force and later attached to the special unit. After that - speaking in general terms - I acquainted Trajkovic with that decision, as well as the police administration, which otherwise is tasked with the manning of the reserve force and their engagement. I told both the commander and the police administration that they should deal with the issue of engagement of those men as part of the MUP reserve force in technical terms and that they should be equipped and issued with arms as well as to put them at the disposal of the special unit, much the way it was done with other units otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have a dilemma now on how to proceed. Could we go into closed session, please, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Closed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, did you know what the destination of the reserve forces that had been attached to the special unit was?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the information I received from the police administration, I knew that the members of reserve forces would be brought to the territory of Kosovo but on this side, and that they would be there awaiting further instructions from the staff in order to join the Special Anti-Terrorist Unit whose reserve forces they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain to us what it means "on this side." Is it this side of the border?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that they could not just enter the territory of Kosovo without a prior decision of the staff, without a prior decision on engaging them in that area. That means that they remained in the territory of Serbia proper and were waiting there for the order to join the special unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Djordjevic, did you know why they were supposed to be stationed in Serbia proper? Do you know what it is that they were awaiting, that they -- why were they waiting for the decision before being transferred to the territory of Kosovo and Metohija and before joining the SAJ?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just knew that they would be on this side and that they would wait for a further order from the staff in order to be attached to the Special Anti-Terrorist Unit. So they were on this side of the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know who made the decision to send the reserve forces from Prolom Banja to the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, and do you know where they were sent, when, and what was the occasion?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally, later on, I learned - and it was the only possible way it could have happened - namely, that it was done pursuant to the decision of the staff. Nobody asked me to make a decision on that nor did I make the decision to have them join the Special Anti-Terrorist Unit nor did I issue any such order, that is to say that they acted upon the decision of the staff and the staff - as I have learned later - sent some men there to conduct the preparations necessary for them to join the special unit and for them to be engaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us when did you learn, what did you learn, and from whom did you learn about how it transpired that the reserve forces of the ministry were sent to Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no personal knowledge, I had none at that point in time. This means that for the moment they came to the location pursuant to the order of the staff, until that time I knew nothing. I don't know when this order was made to have them join the SAJ. The first time I learned of them joining the SAJ was after some members of those reserve forces committed some crimes down there. On the 28th, when this crime was committed, I learned that they had come to the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us how you learned of this, from whom, and what actually happened?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prior to that -- I need to say that one or two days prior to that Trajkovic, the SAJ commander, came across a mine; he was wounded and hospitalised. So I learned about what these reservists had done from the commander of the Belgrade portion of the SAJ, Zoran Simovic, who, following that event and all the measures that had been undertaken until that moment, called me and told me about the crime that the members of reserve forces had committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he tell you what he, Mr. Simovic, did following the crime which took place?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was visibly agitated, and he told me that on that occasion they killed a dozen or more persons, that the special unit provided first aid to those who were wounded, transported them to a hospital and did whatever else was needed, that he immediately informed the staff about the incident, and that upon the order of the staff, he gathered all those reservists and immediately sent them back to the position at which those reservists had been prior to that, that is to say, to the territory of Serbia proper. He also told me that the territorial OUP in Podujevo was also informed about the incident and that they had undertaken measures to document everything, to conduct an on-site investigation, and to continue putting in place measures necessary to secure evidence. I accepted everything that he told me, all the information that he provided, because everything had already been undertaken, all the necessary measures. That is to say, the unit had been sent back pursuant to the staff decision and that they undertook steps to document everything and to conduct an on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: First of all, when he told you about this crime, did he tell you who the victims were?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he told me that those were ethnic Albanian civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. He informed you after all these measures had already been taken. Do you know why he called you specifically?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me on that occasion again that this whole process of involving reservists and reinforcing the SAJ, that this was told him by General Trajkovic and that with regard to the engagement of the reservists and since Trajkovic was wounded at the time and he knew everything, he wanted to inform me as well. He was in such a state of mind that he probably wanted to share that with me as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And this unit was sent back from Kosovo and Metohija to the territory of the administrative part of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Practically, they committed this crime during the first 20 minutes or half an hour that they were there, whilst already they had not been technically attached to the SAJ as reservists. And these reservists immediately thereafter were again collected and sent back to the place where they had been before going into Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you inform anyone about what you heard from Mr. Simovic?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I informed the minister. The minister told me that he had already heard from the staff about this event and that, pursuant to the staff decision, the process of returning these reservists as members of the SAJ was in progress.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now have document 003-1467, and that's 1225 according to 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And it's tab 135 in your binder, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1436. Let me repeat the number: it's D003-1436.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, did you know that an investigating judge conducted a crime scene investigation?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you know that other operational actions were taken to detect the perpetrators of this crime?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that this was done, and, in that respect, certain measures were taken at a later stage in order to find out who did this and to establish their criminal responsibility. There were lots of problems in uncovering the truth, but eventually the whole incident was processed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: We see that the on-site investigation was conducted on the 30th of March, 1999. Do you know why it took all this time between the commission of the crime to the compiling an on-site investigation report?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know the reason for that. I know that the incident took place on the 28th of March. I don't know why they waited to carry out the crime scene investigation on the 30th, which means that more than 24 hours had elapsed since the incident. I don't know the reason for that. All I know is that the on-site investigation was to be conducted properly and that evidence was to be collected for further prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D441.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, we heard that these reservists that had been attached to the SAJ were brought back to the territory of Serbia. What happened next with regard to how they were treated? Do you know anything about that? And if you do, please tell us.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These reservists remained in the same location where they had been before. I think that was in Prolom Banja in the facilities that had previously been used to accommodate the units before they crossed over to Kosovo. So they remained in those facilities for a few days. I also know that a number of them, after they had been brought back from Kosovo, had left these facilities. And a few days later, based on the minister's decision, an order -- or, actually, I issued an order for this reserve force to be sent home. They were instructed to return the weapons that had been issued to them, and it was acted in accordance with my order. The unit commander, Trajkovic, personally carried out this. He went to the facility that they had been staying in and conveyed these orders that I had given him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After this injury took place, were you in contact with Mr. Trajkovic?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were the days of the fiercest bombing of Serbia, of all its towns and cities. So whenever Trajkovic called him [as interpreted], that is when I spoke to him. Otherwise, I had no reason to maintain any contact with him specifically. Whenever he felt he needed something from me, he would call me and ask for certain issues to be resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: After he had been injured, did Trajkovic go to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was in Belgrade, and that happened after he spent a few days in Pristina. He arrived in Belgrade, and he got in touch with me, and we met.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, on page 45, line 15, it says here whenever you called Mr. Trajkovic. Would you please confirm: Did you call Mr. Trajkovic, or was it the other way around?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Trajkovic called me whenever he needed something; therefore, it was his initiative to establish contact with me. However, if I needed him, I would call him. But basically it was him who called me to tell me about his problems and possibly help him with solving them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can we continue where you stopped. You said that upon his return to Belgrade, Mr. Trajkovic called you and you met. Can you tell me what you talked about?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our first contacts were related to the return of the reservists from the SAJ, from their facility in Prolom Banja, that is, about their return home. After that, we would meet whenever he needed certain manpower for Kosovo and Metohija. He would come again and wished and proposed for a number of reservists to be engaged again. Therefore, the disarming of the reservists, or, rather, the return of their weapons did not have the effect of seizing their status of the MUP reserve force. So they retained their status as such. In view of the fact that his unit was expected to be engaged in some broader actions down there, he proposed and requested that a number of these reservists be re-activated and that for his conduct and behaviour down there he would be personally responsible and that everything would go smoothly. That is how it happened that a number of reservists were recruited again within the MUP for the SAJ. And during their repeated recruitment at the assistance of Commander Trajkovic and -- or so the decision of the minister and my participation in this whole matter, they were engaged for two weeks down there until the completion of this wide operation in which the special unit and some hundred members of the reserve force of the special unit took part in. After this engagement which lasted for two weeks, this unit was returned, that is to say, the special unit was returned along with members of its reserve force.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please repeat what was your role in the sending back of these reservists to Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This could not have been done without the minister's decision. Therefore, when Trajkovic proposed to me to re-engage them, I, of course, went to see the minister again; I presented the problem to him; and he gave his approval for re-engaging the members of the MUP reserve for the needs of the SAJ. And, of course, the whole procedure was conducted technically by Mr. Trajkovic and part of the police administration who was in charge of recruiting reservists.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now without mentioning any names in order to avoid going into closed session, when you talked with Trajkovic about demobilising the reserve force following their return to Prolom Banja, do you know whether Mr. Trajkovic went alone to fulfil this task?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He made a proposition at the time that his friend who had been involved in the selection of these reservists to accompany him, due to the fact that the both of them knew very well this man who was the leader of these reservists before they were attached to the special unit. I agreed with this proposition, that is to say that the two of them should try and finish this in the safest possible way, that is, to have them return their weapons and to make sure that no incidents occur. Therefore, I agreed for the two of them to go down there, to accomplish this mission, and that is what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you ever met Mr. Slobodan Medic?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
